problem_statement:
1. Title
Optimization: Multiple URLResolver instances constructed by django.urls.resolvers.get_resolver when set_urlconf not yet called

2. Description
Multiple URLResolver instances can be constructed by django.urls.resolvers.get_resolver if django.urls.base.set_urlconf has not yet been called. get_resolver is memoized with functools.lru_cache and caches resolvers keyed by the urlconf argument. If get_resolver is called once before request handling (when get_urlconf returns None) and again after request handling (when set_urlconf has been called and get_urlconf returns settings.ROOT_URLCONF), two separate URLResolver instances are created and each runs URLResolver._populate. _populate can be expensive for applications with many routes and stores computed caches on the instance, so constructing and populating two resolvers wastes time and memory. A simple mitigation is for get_resolver to resolve settings.ROOT_URLCONF before invoking the memoized function so the same resolver is reused.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Have a Django project with a large number of URL routes (so URLResolver._populate is noticeably expensive).
- Cause get_resolver to be called before any request handling. For example, call django.urls.reverse at import time in some module, which calls get_urlconf -> None -> get_resolver(None).
- Start handling an HTTP request via Django's BaseHandler.get_response. The first request handling calls set_urlconf and associates the current thread/request with settings.ROOT_URLCONF.
- Call django.urls.reverse (or another code path that calls get_resolver) again after set_urlconf has been executed.
- Observe that URLResolver._populate was executed twice and two distinct URLResolver instances (one for None and one for settings.ROOT_URLCONF) were created and cached by lru_cache.

4. Expected Behavior
get_resolver should return and cache a single URLResolver for the project's root URLconf in typical application usage, avoiding redundant construction and expensive _populate calls when code calls get_resolver both before and after the first request handling. Ideally, code paths that call get_resolver before set_urlconf should resolve to the same resolver used after set_urlconf when settings.ROOT_URLCONF is the intended global urlconf.

5. Actual Behavior
When get_resolver is called before set_urlconf, it constructs and caches a URLResolver for None. When called later after set_urlconf, it constructs and caches a second URLResolver for settings.ROOT_URLCONF. URLResolver._populate runs for each instance, duplicating expensive work and storing redundant instance caches.

6. Severity/Priority
Performance: Medium–High. Causes redundant expensive work (double _populate) and increased memory usage in projects with many routes. Priority: High for large projects or libraries that call reverse at import time.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Django applications with large route trees where URLResolver._populate is expensive.
- Code that calls django.urls.reverse (or other get_resolver call-sites) both at import time (or before first request) and during/after request handling.
- Any multi-threaded or long-running processes where set_urlconf is not set prior to some early calls to get_resolver.

8. Environment
- Django internals: django.urls.resolvers.get_resolver, URLResolver._populate, django.urls.base.set_urlconf, BaseHandler.get_response, django.urls.resolvers.get_urlconf
- Python: functools.lru_cache used to memoize get_resolver
- Typical deployment where settings.ROOT_URLCONF is used as the project urlconf

9. Additional Information
- Current behavior stems from get_resolver being memoized and keyed on the urlconf argument; None and settings.ROOT_URLCONF are different keys, so two resolvers are cached.
- Proposed fix: modify get_resolver to look up settings.ROOT_URLCONF before the memoized function call so the cached resolver uses the real root urlconf instead of None when appropriate.
- The reporter plans to contribute a patch once the Contributor License Agreement (CLA) is signed.

problem_statement:
1. Title
RelatedFieldListFilter and RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter do not respect related model Meta.ordering (ordering lost or omitted)

2. Description
RelatedFieldListFilter clears or fails to inherit ordering and does not fall back to the related model's Model._meta.ordering. In django/contrib/admin/filters.py (v2.2.1) ordering is set to an empty tuple and remains empty unless the related model has an explicit ModelAdmin.ordering defined. RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter does not pass any ordering to field.get_choices and therefore does not apply ordering defined on the related model's ModelAdmin or the model's Meta.ordering. The filters should respect the related model's Meta.ordering when no explicit ModelAdmin.ordering is provided, and should pass ordering to get_choices.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Use Django 2.2.1 admin with a model A that has a ForeignKey to model B.
- Define ordering on model B via class Meta: ordering = ('name',) (no ModelAdmin.ordering for B).
- Register model A in the admin and use the default RelatedFieldListFilter or RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter for the ForeignKey filter.
- Observe the admin filter choices for the related model B are not ordered according to B._meta.ordering.
- Inspect code paths:
  - RelatedFieldListFilter sets ordering = () (filters.py around line 196).
  - RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter calls field.get_choices without an ordering kwarg (filters.py around line 422).

4. Expected Behavior
- If a related model's ModelAdmin.ordering is not set, RelatedFieldListFilter and RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter should fall back to the related model's Meta.ordering (Model._meta.ordering) for ordering the filter choices.
- RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter should pass an ordering argument to field.get_choices so that ordering is applied consistently.

5. Actual Behavior
- RelatedFieldListFilter sets ordering to an empty tuple and does not fall back to Model._meta.ordering; the filter choices are unordered or not in the expected model-defined order.
- RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter omits the ordering kwarg when calling field.get_choices, so the related model's ordering is ignored entirely.

6. Severity/Priority
Medium — affects admin usability and expected ordering of related object filters; may confuse users relying on model-level ordering.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Django 2.2.x admin users who use RelatedFieldListFilter or RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter for related model fields.
- Projects that rely on Model.Meta.ordering (Model._meta.ordering) instead of setting ordering on ModelAdmin.

8. Environment
- Django 2.2.1 (observed)
- Files/lines referenced:
  - django/contrib/admin/filters.py line ~196 (RelatedFieldListFilter ordering set to empty tuple)
  - django/contrib/admin/filters.py line ~422 (RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter calling field.get_choices without ordering kwarg)

9. Additional Information
- The problem can be addressed by:
  - Making RelatedFieldListFilter fall back to the related model's Model._meta.ordering when ModelAdmin.ordering is not defined.
  - Ensuring RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter passes the ordering kwarg to field.get_choices so that the related model or ModelAdmin ordering is applied.
- Relevant behavior and call sites are in the admin filters implementation linked above; patching these areas to respect Model._meta.ordering and to include ordering in get_choices would restore expected behavior.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Allow cleaned_data to overwrite model field default values when the field is absent from the submitted data

2. Description
When a form is submitted and a field is not present in the request payload (for example because the field is omitted from the form or its value is derived from another field), a model field that has a default value cannot be set from self.cleaned_data. The cleaned_data modification paradigm implies that values set in clean()/clean_<field>() should be applied, but currently the model's default value can remain instead. This forces authors to manually copy/overwrite the raw submitted data instead of relying on cleaned_data. See related discussion: https://github.com/django/django/pull/7068/files#r289432409

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Define a model with a field that has a default value, e.g. some_field = models.CharField(default='DEFAULT').
- Define a ModelForm that does not include some_field in the rendered form (or omit the field from the POST data).
- In the form's clean() or clean_some_field(), set self.cleaned_data['some_field'] to a new value.
- Save the form (form.save()).
- Observe that the saved model instance has the model default ('DEFAULT') for some_field instead of the value set in cleaned_data.

4. Expected Behavior
If cleaned_data contains a value for a field (either set by user input or set programmatically in clean()/clean_<field>()), that value should be used to populate the model field on save(), even when the original POST data did not include the field and the model field has a default value.

5. Actual Behavior
The model field retains its model-defined default value when the field was not present in the submitted data, even if self.cleaned_data contains a different value for that field. cleaned_data changes are not applied in this case.

6. Severity/Priority
High — this breaks the expected behavior of form cleaning and can lead to incorrect data being saved when fields are derived or omitted from the form input.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Developers using Django ModelForm (or forms that save model instances) where some fields are omitted from the submitted payload or automatically derived.
- Any system relying on form.clean()/clean_<field>() to programmatically set/override field values when those fields are not present in the POST data.

8. Environment
- Django forms/ModelForm save flow (issue discovered and discussed in PR context: https://github.com/django/django/pull/7068).
- No specific OS/DB dependency; behavior is in form/model save logic and is framework-level.

9. Additional Information
- Reproduction can be implemented with a small Model/ModelForm example that omits a field from the rendered form and sets it in clean().
- Two possible remediation approaches:
  - Ensure form.save() (or the model instance population step) prefers values from cleaned_data when present, regardless of whether the field existed in the raw POST.
  - Document the current behavior clearly if the change is not desired.
- See original discussion for context: https://github.com/django/django/pull/7068/files#r289432409

problem_statement:
1. Title
ModelBackend.authenticate() performs unnecessary database query and password hashing when username is None

2. Description
ModelBackend.authenticate() currently performs a database lookup even when the supplied username is None (and also runs the default password hasher in the failure path). This results in a useless SQL query such as SELECT ... WHERE "auth_user"."username" IS NULL and an unnecessary cost of running UserModel().set_password(password). The extra work is avoidable when username or password are None (for example when credentials are intended for a different authentication backend). A simple early return when username or password is None would avoid the query and expensive hashing.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Install or run tests that use multiple authentication backends (for example a project using django-sesame alongside ModelBackend).
- Call authenticate(request, username=None, password=None, ...) or otherwise invoke ModelBackend.authenticate with username=None (this can happen when other backends are being tried).
- Observe queries logged or assertNumQueries: you will see a query like:
  SELECT ... FROM "auth_user" WHERE "auth_user"."username" IS NULL
- Observe that UserModel().set_password(password) is invoked (password hashing work) in the failure path.

4. Expected Behavior
If username is None or password is None, ModelBackend.authenticate should not query the user table and should return None immediately (no database query, no unnecessary password hashing), allowing other backends to run without incurring extra cost from ModelBackend.

5. Actual Behavior
ModelBackend.authenticate attempts to resolve the user by calling UserModel._default_manager.get_by_natural_key(username) even when username is None, producing a SQL query filtering username IS NULL (username is not nullable so the query is pointless). If the lookup fails, it runs UserModel().set_password(password) to exercise the password hasher — an expensive operation — even though credentials were likely intended for another backend.

6. Severity/Priority
Medium. This causes unnecessary database activity and CPU work (password hashing) in multi-backend authentication scenarios and can lead to slower authentication flows and noisy tests. It is not a security vulnerability by itself but is a performance/efficiency bug.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Projects that use Django's ModelBackend together with other authentication backends (e.g., django-sesame or custom backends).
- Test suites that assert query counts (assertNumQueries) which will see an extra, pointless query.
- Any system where authenticate() may be called with username=None or password=None as part of trying multiple backends.

8. Environment
- Django's ModelBackend.authenticate implementation as currently implemented at time of report (the version where authenticate does get_by_natural_key(username) and calls set_password on failure).
- Any database backend (observed SQL: WHERE "auth_user"."username" IS NULL).
- Example consumer: django-sesame (testing scenario).

9. Additional Information
- Current code comment indicates the password hasher is run to reduce timing differences between existing and non-existing users. However, when multiple authentication backends are used, different backends inherently cause timing differences, so masking timing at this point is of limited value and causes unnecessary cost.
- Proposed change: add an early return to skip lookup and hashing when username or password is None, for example:
  if username is None or password is None:
      return
- This reduces wasted DB queries and avoids running the expensive password hasher in cases where credentials are not intended for ModelBackend.

problem_statement:
1. Title
translate_url() produces incorrect URL when optional named groups are missing from the input URL

2. Description
translate_url() fails to produce the correct translated URL when the source URL pattern contains optional named capture groups and those optional groups are absent in the URL being translated. The function either leaves placeholders or extra delimiters in the result instead of omitting the optional portion as expected. This issue is observed in a unit test included with the patch.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Define a URL pattern that includes an optional named capture group, for example a pattern where a language or optional segment is wrapped in an optional group.
- Call translate_url() (the function responsible for translating/rewriting URLs) with a URL that does not include the optional segment.
- Observe the returned translated URL.

4. Expected Behavior
When an optional named group is not present in the input URL, translate_url() should produce a translated URL that omits the optional portion entirely, producing a correct, canonical URL without leftover placeholders, "None" text, or superfluous delimiters (e.g., extra slashes).

5. Actual Behavior
translate_url() returns an incorrect URL containing remnants of the optional group (such as placeholders, extraneous characters, or malformed delimiters) when the optional named group is missing from the input URL. This results in an invalid or unexpected URL.

6. Severity/Priority
Severity: Medium — causes incorrect URLs to be generated which may break routing, links, or i18n behavior.
Priority: High enough to fix before release if URL translation is relied upon in the codebase or tests.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Any application code that uses translate_url() for URL translation/rewriting, particularly where URL patterns include optional named groups.
- Automated tests that exercise translate_url() with optional groups (the failing test in the patch demonstrates this).
- Users relying on translated links for navigation, internationalization, or redirects.

8. Environment
- Function: translate_url() within the project's URL translation module (exact module/reference available in repository).
- Observed in unit test included with the patch.
- No specific OS or runtime constraints identified; issue is tied to URL pattern handling logic rather than platform.

9. Additional Information
- The failing behavior is reproducible in the provided test case in the patch.
- Potential workarounds: ensure optional segments are handled explicitly by translate_url() callers (e.g., pass empty strings for optional named groups) or avoid optional named groups in critical URL patterns until the issue is fixed.
- Recommended next step: inspect how translate_url() constructs the translated URL from named groups and adjust logic to skip or remove optional group fragments when the group is missing or empty.

Could you please provide the patch as a pull request against master? Unless this is a regression, it probably doesn't qualify for a backport to 1.9 (see our ​supported versions policy). Please check the patch on Python 3 as well (dict.iteritems() doesn't exist there).
The issue here is that resolve() will return None for any optional capture groups that aren't captured, but reverse() will use force_text() and convert it to the literal string 'None'. This causes an asymmetry between resolve() and reverse(). I think it's a better idea to treat this asymmetry as a bug, and solve it within reverse(). We would discard any arguments that are None. Incidentally this will allow for cleaner code when you don't know if an optional parameter is set when you call reverse() or the {% url %} template tag: {% if obj.might_be_none != None %} {% url 'my_view' obj.might_be_none %} {% else %} {% url 'my_view' %} {% endif %} vs. {% url 'my_view' obj.might_be_none %} I think that's a reasonably common usecase, so it would be nice to support this cleaner syntax. Non-existent template variables will still pass an empty string rather than None, so this won't hide any typos in your template variable names.
This also affects the set_language function. When changing language on a page with an URL pattern containing an optional group, the empty optional part is set to none and translating the page leads to a 404. The bug on translation did not exist back in 1.8, not sure when it was introduced. I'm on 2.2. The best way to resolve both issues would be to patch directly _reverse_with_prefix in django.urls.resolvers.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Composed queries ignore changes to selected columns when values()/values_list() is called multiple times (e.g., union(qs, qs).values_list())

2. Description
When a composed QuerySet (for example produced by union()) has values() or values_list() evaluated multiple times with different field lists, the second evaluation does not reflect the new list of columns. Instead it returns the columns from the first evaluation. Example: calling .values_list('name', 'order') first and then .values_list('order') still yields both columns. The behavior appears in compiler.py around lines 428-433.

3. Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a record:
   >>> ReservedName.objects.create(name='a', order=2)
2. Build a QuerySet and compose it with itself:
   >>> qs1 = ReservedName.objects.all()
3. Evaluate values_list for two columns:
   >>> print(qs1.union(qs1).values_list('name', 'order').get())
   ('a', 2)
4. Evaluate values_list for one column on the same composed expression pattern:
   >>> print(qs1.union(qs1).values_list('order').get())
   ('a', 2)

4. Expected Behavior
The second call to values_list('order') should return a single-element tuple ('a',) or the scalar 2 depending on flat argument, i.e., only the requested 'order' column should be returned.

5. Actual Behavior
The second call still returns both columns ('a', 2) — the result reflects the column list from the earlier values_list call instead of the newly requested column list.

6. Severity/Priority
High — leads to incorrect query results and can silently return wrong columns for composed queries, causing data integrity and application logic errors.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Users of Django ORM composing QuerySets (union(), intersection, difference, etc.)
- Codepaths that call values() or values_list() on composed QuerySets multiple times with different column selections
- Libraries or applications that build queries dynamically and rely on a fresh projection per values()/values_list() call

8. Environment
- Observed in Django ORM query compiler (see compiler.py around lines 428-433)
- No specific Django version provided in original report; likely affects versions with the referenced compiler.py implementation
- Reproducible in a typical Django environment with a model ReservedName having fields name and order

9. Additional Information
- The problem appears related to composed query compilation/caching where the output column list is reused across multiple evaluations instead of being recomputed for the new projection.
- Relevant code region: compiler.py#L428-L433 (as noted by reporter).
- Minimal reproduction shown above; further debugging should inspect how output fields/annotations are stored and reused during compilation of combined queries.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Email construction crashes with Unicode hostname when email.encoding is non-Unicode (e.g., iso-8859-1) — Message-ID header triggers UnicodeEncodeError

2. Description
When the system hostname (used as DNS_NAME for Message-ID) contains non-ASCII characters (for example "正宗" or "漢字") and an EmailMessage has a non-Unicode encoding (for example 'iso-8859-1'), constructing the email message triggers a UnicodeEncodeError. The failure occurs because Django passes the raw Unicode domain into the Message-ID header and the header encoding logic attempts to encode it using the configured email encoding rather than converting the domain to ASCII-compatible encoding (Punycode). This causes mail-related tests to fail and will break email generation on systems with non-ASCII hostnames.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Set the machine hostname (or mock DNS_NAME) to a non-ASCII value, e.g. "正宗" or "漢字".
- Create an EmailMessage:
  - email = EmailMessage('subject', '', 'from@example.com', ['to@example.com'])
  - email.encoding = 'iso-8859-1'
- Call message = email.message() (this triggers generating the Message-ID header).
- Observe the UnicodeEncodeError raised during header encoding.
- Equivalent failing test: tests/mail/tests.py::test_unicode_dns in Django master.

4. Expected Behavior
Django should ensure the domain used in Message-ID and other headers is safe for ASCII-only headers when email.encoding is a non-Unicode charset. Specifically:
- Convert the domain name to Punycode (IDNA / "xn--" form) before inserting it into headers such as Message-ID.
- Header encoding should succeed with the configured email.encoding (iso-8859-1) and not raise UnicodeEncodeError.
- The generated Message-ID should contain the Punycode form of the hostname (e.g., 'xn--p8s937b').

5. Actual Behavior
A UnicodeEncodeError is raised during header construction:
- The header value (Message-ID containing the Unicode domain) is passed to email.header.Header with charset=iso-8859-1.
- The header encoding attempts to encode the Unicode domain using 'latin-1' and fails with:
  UnicodeEncodeError: 'latin-1' codec can't encode characters in position ...: ordinal not in range(256)
- Result: email.message() fails and tests crash.

6. Severity/Priority
High — breaks email construction on systems with non-ASCII hostnames when email.encoding is not Unicode; causes test failures and can prevent sending/creating messages in real deployments.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Any Django project that runs on a host with a non-ASCII hostname (or otherwise sets DNS_NAME to a non-ASCII domain) and that generates emails with a non-Unicode email.encoding (e.g., 'iso-8859-1').
- Django test suite that includes tests relying on DNS_NAME and email encoding.
- Likely affects all platforms where hostname can be non-ASCII (Linux, macOS, Windows).

8. Environment
- Django: master branch (tests reference tests/mail/tests.py)
- Python: 3.7.3 (trace shows /usr/local/Cellar/python/3.7.3/Frameworks/...)
- Example local paths in traceback: /Users/chason/projects/django/...
- Hostname/DNS_NAME example values: "正宗", "漢字"
- Email encoding used in reproduction: 'iso-8859-1' (latin-1)

9. Additional Information
Suggested fix:
- Convert domain names to Punycode (IDNA) before inserting them into headers (e.g., in django.core.mail.utils or django.core.mail.message). This ensures headers remain ASCII and are safe to encode with non-Unicode email encodings.

problem_statement:
1. Title
admin.E108 incorrectly raised for fields accessible only via instance (e.g., PositionField) after Django 2.2.1 change

2. Description
After upgrading from Django 2.0.7 to 2.2.1, ModelAdmin list_display validation started raising admin.E108 incorrectly for a field that is valid but only accessible via model instances (a descriptor that raises when accessed on the model class). A PositionField from django-positions is an example: accessing the attribute on the model class raises, but accessing it on an instance works. A change in commit 47016ad... (related to ticket 28490) altered _check_list_display_item so that hasattr(model, item) being false prevents attempting model._meta.get_field(item). This causes a false positive E108 when get_field would have succeeded or when the attribute is valid only at instance level. The bug prevents Django from starting due to admin checks failing.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Install Django 2.2.1 and django-positions (or use a custom descriptor field that raises when accessed on the model class).
- Define model and admin as follows:
  from django.db import models
  from position.Fields import PositionField

  class Thing(models.Model):
      number = models.IntegerField(default=0)
      order = PositionField()

  from django.contrib import admin
  from .models import Thing

  @admin.register(Thing)
  class ThingAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
      list_display = ['number', 'order']

- Start the Django project (runserver or other startup).
- Observe that admin checks raise admin.E108: "The value of list_display[1] refers to 'order' which is not a callable..." and startup is prevented.

Notes: Under Django 2.0.7 the same code starts successfully. Changing the field names to ones that truly do not exist yields the correct validation errors; the problem is specific to attributes where getattr on the class raises or hasattr returns False while get_field should recognise the field.

4. Expected Behavior
Django admin list_display validation should:
- Accept 'order' in list_display when the model defines a field (via _meta.get_field) even if accessing the attribute on the model class with getattr raises or hasattr returns False.
- Only raise admin.E108 when the item is neither a callable, an attribute of the ModelAdmin, nor an attribute or method of the model (i.e., both getattr on the class and model._meta.get_field fail).
- Raise admin.E109 only when the resolved field is a ManyToManyField.

5. Actual Behavior
Django 2.2.1's _check_list_display_item returns admin.E108 in cases where hasattr(model, item) is False (because getattr on the class raises) and the code short-circuits without attempting model._meta.get_field(item). This produces a false admin.E108 (and prevents startup) for fields like PositionField that are valid for instances but not accessible on the class.

6. Severity/Priority
High — blocks Django startup/admin from running when a valid list_display field is present but is accessible only via instances (e.g., PositionField), which affects production and development workflows.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Projects using django-admin with list_display that reference descriptor-like fields which raise or return None when accessed on the model class (e.g., django-positions PositionField).
- Any custom descriptor fields or attributes only available on model instances.
- Users upgrading from Django 2.0.x to 2.2.x who rely on such fields.

8. Environment
- Django: 2.2.1 (problem present); 2.0.7 (no problem)
- Affected field example: django-positions PositionField
- Code change reference: commit 47016adbf54b54143d4cf052eeb29fc72d27e6b1
- Related ticket: https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/28490
- Python/OS: not specified in original report

9. Additional Information
- Root cause: The change intended to fix ticket 28490 introduced an early check of hasattr(model, item). If hasattr is False because getattr on the model class raises (descriptor behavior), the code returns E108 without attempting model._meta.get_field(item). This conflates different failure modes and prevents correct handling of fields discoverable via model._meta.get_field.
- Suggested fix: Remove the early hasattr(model, item) short-circuit and attempt model._meta.get_field(item) first (or at least try get_field even if hasattr is False). Only return admin.E108 when both get_field raises FieldDoesNotExist and getattr(model, item) raises AttributeError. Check for ManyToManyField from the resolved field as before. The original reporter provided a replacement _check_list_display_item implementation that exhibits the correct behavior in all tested cases.
- Reproduction and diagnosis notes: Changing list_display names and comparing behavior between 2.0.7 and 2.2.1 helps confirm the regression. The problem is deterministic for descriptor fields that throw on class access.
- Links:
  - Commit: https://github.com/django/django/commit/47016adbf54b54143d4cf052eeb29fc72d27e6b1
  - Ticket: https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/28490

problem_statement:
1. Title
order_by() on parent model crashes when Meta.ordering contains expressions (multi-table inheritance, occurs during test DB setup)

2. Description
During testing I discovered a crash when using a query expression for ordering on a model involved in multi-table inheritance. When Django builds ordering for the parent model, the code passes an OrderBy object (an expression) into get_order_dir, which expects a string/field name. This causes an exception during test database setup. The issue is reproducible in the example repository: https://github.com/JonnyWaffles/djangoordermetabug. The original report and the failing stacktrace were posted by Jonny Fuller (JonnyWaffles).

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Clone the reproducible test repository: https://github.com/JonnyWaffles/djangoordermetabug
- Install dependencies and configure a test database as described in the repo (or run in an environment matching the repo requirements).
- Run the Django test suite (manage.py test) or otherwise trigger test DB creation.
- Observe that test DB setup crashes when Django evaluates Meta.ordering that contains an expression on a parent model in a multi-table inheritance setup.

4. Expected Behavior
Django should accept expressions in Meta.ordering on models participating in multi-table inheritance and handle them without raising an exception during test database creation or any other code path. get_order_dir should handle ordering expressions (OrderBy objects) appropriately (either by recognizing them as expressions or by converting them to a string/alias that the ordering machinery expects).

5. Actual Behavior
Django raises an exception during test DB setup because get_order_dir receives an OrderBy object (expression) instead of a string/field name and fails when trying to treat it as a field identifier. The crash occurs specifically during test DB setup in the multi-table inheritance case; it does not occur when running in a REPL or a custom script in the reporter's manual testing.

6. Severity/Priority
High priority for affected users: this makes running the test suite fail for projects that use expressions in Meta.ordering on parent models with multi-table inheritance. It blocks test execution and makes CI/test automation unreliable for those cases.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Django projects using Meta.ordering with expressions (e.g., OrderBy, combined expressions) on models that are parents in multi-table inheritance hierarchies.
- Particularly impacts developers running Django tests (test DB setup) or CI systems that run the test suite.
- Likely affects multiple Django versions where Meta.ordering expression handling and multi-table inheritance interact (see repo for reproduction).

8. Environment
- Repro repository: https://github.com/JonnyWaffles/djangoordermetabug
- Observed when running Django test DB setup (manage.py test).
- Exact Django/Python versions not specified in the original report; reproduce using the versions pinned or implied in the reproducible repository. The reporter observed the difference between behavior in REPL/script vs. test DB setup.

9. Additional Information
- The core cause appears to be that the ordering field value is an OrderBy object (an expression) rather than a plain string when get_order_dir is called.
- The linked stacktrace in the original report demonstrates the failure path (see the repository and the issue write-up for the trace).
- The failure only occurred during test DB setup in the reporter's environment; unclear why the code path differs from REPL/script usage.
- Contributor: Jonny Fuller (JonnyWaffles) provided the initial report and reproduction repository.
- Repository and test cases should be sufficient for maintainers to reproduce and diagnose the root cause. Any fix should ensure get_order_dir and the ordering machinery can safely handle expressions (OrderBy) in Meta.ordering for multi-table inheritance and during test DB setup.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Support DISTINCT in Avg and Sum aggregates

2. Description
As an extension of issue #28658, the general aggregate functions Avg and Sum should accept the DISTINCT modifier. Prior to version 2.2 these aggregates silently ignored the DISTINCT parameter; starting with 2.2 they throw an exception when DISTINCT is used. The change required is to mark the Avg and Sum classes as allowing DISTINCT. This same change could also be applied to Min and Max, though it is less important for those.

problem_statement:
1. Title
simplify_regexp()/replace_named_groups fails to replace final named group when pattern lacks trailing '/'

2. Description
replace_named_groups() (used by simplify_regexp()) fails to replace the final named capture group if the provided urlpattern string does not end with a trailing '/'. Example pattern r'entries/(?P<pk>[^/.]+)/relationships/(?P<related_field>\w+)' leaves the "related_field" group unreplaced. Adding a trailing '/' to the pattern is a workaround that causes the replacement to succeed. This function is used downstream in Django REST Framework (see issue 6888).

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Call replace_named_groups() or simplify_regexp() with the pattern:
  r'entries/(?P<pk>[^/.]+)/relationships/(?P<related_field>\w+)'
- Observe the output.
- Repeat with a trailing slash appended:
  r'entries/(?P<pk>[^/.]+)/relationships/(?P<related_field>\w+)/'
- Observe that the replacement succeeds when the trailing slash is present.

4. Expected Behavior
All named capture groups in the input pattern, including the final group, should be replaced properly regardless of whether the pattern ends with a trailing '/'.

5. Actual Behavior
The final named capture group ("related_field" in the example) is not replaced when the input pattern lacks a trailing '/'. The same input with a trailing '/' is processed correctly.

6. Severity/Priority
Medium — affects URL pattern simplification used by downstream projects (e.g., Django REST Framework). Causes incorrect output for patterns that omit a trailing slash, which is a common case.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Projects and users that rely on simplify_regexp() or replace_named_groups(), notably Django REST Framework consumers.
- Any code that generates or manipulates URL patterns without a trailing '/'.

8. Environment
- Function appears in the codebase that provides simplify_regexp()/replace_named_groups(); observed in workflows involving Django REST Framework (referenced issue 6888).
- Reproduction is independent of a specific Python/Django version in the original report; the issue is tied to the pattern string format (presence/absence of trailing '/').

9. Additional Information
- Example problematic input: r'entries/(?P<pk>[^/.]+)/relationships/(?P<related_field>\w+)'
- Workaround: append a trailing '/' to the pattern so it becomes:
  r'entries/(?P<pk>[^/.]+)/relationships/(?P<related_field>\w+)/'
- The original report included code that reproduces the problem and references DRF issue 6888.

problem_statement:
1. Title
OuterRef used inside exclude() or ~Q() resolves to wrong model and raises ValueError

2. Description
A test added to tests/queries/test_qs_combinators fails when using OuterRef() inside an exclude() or inside a negated Q() (~Q(...)) within a subquery (Exists). Using the same OuterRef() inside filter() works as expected, but wrapping the predicate in exclude() or ~Q() causes Django to raise a ValueError claiming the queryset contains a reference to an outer query and may only be used in a subquery. The failure indicates that the OuterRef is being resolved or validated against the wrong query context when used in exclude()/~Q().

3. Steps to Reproduce
1. Add the following test (or run equivalent code) in tests/queries/test_qs_combinators:
   def test_exists_exclude(self):
       # filter()
       qs = Number.objects.annotate(
           foo=Exists(
               Item.objects.filter(tags__category_id=OuterRef('pk'))
           )
       ).filter(foo=True)
       print(qs) # works

       # exclude()
       qs = Number.objects.annotate(
           foo =Exists(
               Item.objects.exclude(tags__category_id=OuterRef('pk'))
           )
       ).filter(foo=True)
       print(qs) # crashes

       # filter(~Q())
       qs = Number.objects.annotate(
           foo =Exists(
               Item.objects.filter(~Q(tags__category_id=OuterRef('pk')))
           )
       ).filter(foo=True)
       print(qs) # crashes

2. Run the test.

4. Expected Behavior
Using OuterRef('pk') inside subquery predicates should be allowed regardless of whether the predicate is expressed with filter(), exclude(), or a negated Q(). The Exists(...) annotation should work and the queryset should be built and executed without raising a ValueError.

5. Actual Behavior
The first case (filter with OuterRef) succeeds. The second and third cases (exclude with OuterRef, filter with ~Q(OuterRef)) raise:
ValueError: This queryset contains a reference to an outer query and may only be used in a subquery

This indicates the ORM treats the OuterRef as an invalid outer reference in these forms.

6. Severity/Priority
High. This breaks valid usage patterns of OuterRef inside subqueries and causes tests and code using exclude() or negated Q predicates with OuterRef to fail.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Developers using the Django ORM features Exists, OuterRef, Subquery with exclude() or negated Q() predicates.
- Test suites referencing similar patterns (e.g., tests/queries/test_qs_combinators).
- Any application logic that relies on negated subquery filters using OuterRef.

8. Environment
- Repository/test file: tests/queries/test_qs_combinators (test_exists_exclude)
- Models involved in the repro: Number, Item with relation tags__category_id referencing Number.pk
- Django ORM (Exists, OuterRef, Q) — exact Django/Python versions not specified in the original report.

9. Additional Information
- The failure only occurs when the OuterRef appears inside exclude() or inside a negated Q(), not when used inside filter().
- Error message: "ValueError: This queryset contains a reference to an outer query and may only be used in a subquery"
- No stack trace was provided in the original report.
- Reproducer code is provided above; adding it as a unit test demonstrates the regression.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Change UUIDField to ForeignKey does not create migration dependency for target app, causing "Related model ... cannot be resolved"

2. Description
When I change a model field from UUIDField to ForeignKey that points to a model in another app, the generated migration does not add a dependency on the target app. Running the test/migrations then raises ValueError: Related model 'testapp2.App2' cannot be resolved. This appears to be a migration bug: a ForeignKey to a model in another app should create a dependency on that app so the related model is available when the migration is applied.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Create a Django project "testproject" with two apps: testapp1 and testapp2.
- Define models as follows:
  - testapp2.models:
    - class App2(models.Model):
        id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, unique=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
        text = models.CharField(max_length=100)
  - testapp1.models:
    - class App1(models.Model):
        id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, unique=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
        text = models.CharField(max_length=100)
        another_app = models.UUIDField(null=True, blank=True)
- Make initial migrations and migrate.
- Modify testapp1.models.App1.another_app to be a ForeignKey:
    another_app = models.ForeignKey(App2, null=True, blank=True, on_delete=models.SET_NULL)
- Run makemigrations for testapp1 to produce a new migration.
- Run the migrations or execute the included test. The code raises:
  ValueError: Related model 'testapp2.App2' cannot be resolved.

4. Expected Behavior
When converting a UUIDField to a ForeignKey referencing a model in another app, makemigrations should add an explicit migration dependency on the target app (testapp2) so the related model (App2) exists/gets migrated before the migration that introduces the ForeignKey. The generated migration should include a dependency entry for testapp2.

5. Actual Behavior
The generated migration for testapp1 does not include a dependency on testapp2. Applying the migration or running the test leads to:
ValueError: Related model 'testapp2.App2' cannot be resolved.

6. Severity/Priority
High - migration correctness and cross-app foreign key resolution are fundamental; failure prevents applying migrations and breaks projects converting fields to relations across apps.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Developers using Django migrations who change a UUIDField (or similar) to a ForeignKey to a model in another app.
- Projects with cross-app ForeignKey changes, especially on Django 2.2 with PostgreSQL (reported environment).

8. Environment
- Django version: 2.2
- Database: PostgreSQL
- Project: "testproject" with apps "testapp1" and "testapp2"
- Attached: an archive with project sources and a small test that reproduces the error (as reported by the reporter).

9. Additional Information
- Error observed: ValueError: Related model 'testapp2.App2' cannot be resolved.
- Reporter: Viktor Lomakin (new to Django community); original post also linked on django-users group: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/django-users/Django$20bug$3A$20change$20uuid$20field$20to$20FK$20does$20not$20create$20dependency%7Csort:date/django-users/-h9LZxFomLU/yz-NLi1cDgAJ
- Note: The issue was last modified by Simon Charette in the original report metadata.
- Request: Verify whether this is a Django bug; if so, makemigrations should create the correct dependency for the ForeignKey target app when converting a non-relational field to a relation.

There's a lot of history in here, so it may turn out this is a duplicate, but I'll accept this for now, as there's certainly a bug. makemigrations generats this: dependencies = [ ('testapp1', '0002_app1_another_app'), ] operations = [ migrations.AlterField( model_name='app1', name='another_app', field=models.ForeignKey(blank=True, null=True, on_delete=django.db.models.deletion.SET_NULL, to='testapp2.App2', verbose_name='another app'), ), ] But that gives the ValueError as you say. Adjusting dependencies allows the test to pass: dependencies = [ ('testapp1', '0002_app1_another_app'), ('testapp2', '0001_initial'), ] Thus, AlterField should pick this up. (Note for later: SQLite will require disabling constraint checking for this, ref #30023.)
That's probably a bug in django.db.migrations.autodetector.MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields's ​call to add_operation which doesn't pass any dependencies when new_field.is_relation and not old_field.is_relation. The dependencies can be retrieved by using self._get_dependencies_for_foreign_key(new_field). We want to depend on the latest migration of the referenced app instead of the initial one though as the model we're referencing might have been altered since then but that's something the aforementioned method should handle. Tests should be added to django/tests/migrations/test_autodetector.py.

problem_statement:
1. Title
call_command ignores kwargs for arguments that are required only via a mutually exclusive group, causing CommandError

2. Description
When calling Django's call_command with a keyword argument that corresponds to an argument which is part of a required mutually exclusive group, call_command does not pass that option through to the parser. As a result the management command raises CommandError complaining that one of the group arguments is required, even though the kwarg was provided. The command works if the option is passed as a raw argv string (e.g. '--shop-id=1') but not when passed as a keyword argument (shop_id=1). The underlying cause appears to be that call_command only forwards options whose parser action has opt.required=True, and it does not consider that a mutually exclusive group can impose requiredness across multiple actions.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Define a management command that sets up a mutually exclusive group required=True:
  shop = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)
  shop.add_argument('--shop-id', nargs='?', type=int, default=None, dest='shop_id')
  shop.add_argument('--shop', nargs='?', type=str, default=None, dest='shop_name')
- Invoke the command programmatically using call_command with a kwarg:
  call_command('my_command', shop_id=1)
- Observe the raised exception:
  django.core.management.base.CommandError: Error: one of the arguments --shop-id --shop is required
- Note that passing the option as an argv string works:
  call_command('my_command', '--shop-id=1')

4. Expected Behavior
call_command should accept keyword arguments corresponding to parser arguments even when those arguments are required only because they belong to a required mutually exclusive group. In the example, call_command('my_command', shop_id=1) should run the command successfully without raising CommandError.

5. Actual Behavior
call_command ignores the provided kwarg because the individual parser actions for --shop-id and --shop are not marked opt.required=True. The method only forwards options whose actions are flagged required, so the mutually exclusive group required constraint is not taken into account. This causes the parser to behave as if no group member was provided and results in a CommandError.

6. Severity/Priority
High / P1 — This breaks programmatic invocation of management commands that use required mutually exclusive argument groups, which is a common use case for testing and automation.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Developers using Django management.call_command to invoke commands programmatically.
- Any management commands that declare required mutually exclusive argument groups.
- Tests and automation scripts that rely on call_command to pass options as kwargs.

8. Environment
- Behavior observed in Django's call_command implementation where parse_args is built from parser._actions and only actions with opt.required are forwarded. (Exact Django version not specified in the report; code path referenced is in management/base.py where parse_args is assembled from required actions.)
- Python/Django environment where management commands use argparse-style add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True).

9. Additional Information
- Relevant code pattern in call_command:
  parse_args += [
    '{}={}'.format(min(opt.option_strings), arg_options[opt.dest])
    for opt in parser._actions if opt.required and opt.dest in options
  ]
  This only checks opt.required on individual actions and ignores group-level requiredness.
- Workaround: pass the option as an argv string to call_command, e.g. call_command('my_command', '--shop-id=1').
- Suggested fix: detect options that belong to a mutually exclusive group which is required and treat their dests as forwards for parse_args, or otherwise include any provided option kwargs in parse_args regardless of opt.required.

problem_statement:
1. Title
AuthenticationForm's username field no longer renders maxlength HTML attribute (regression)

2. Description
AuthenticationForm's username field does not include the maxlength HTML attribute when rendered. This is a regression introduced by change #27515 (commit 5ceaf14686ce626404afb6a5fbd3d8286410bf13). The missing maxlength breaks client-side constraints and HTML validation for forms that rely on the attribute being present.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Use Django version containing the changes from #27515 / commit 5ceaf14686ce626404afb6a5fbd3d8286410bf13 (regression present).
- Instantiate AuthenticationForm (e.g., in a view or shell).
- Render the form's username field (for example, using form.as_p(), form.as_table(), or directly rendering {{ form.username }} in a template).
- Inspect the rendered <input> element for the username field and observe that the maxlength attribute is missing.

4. Expected Behavior
The rendered username <input> should include a maxlength attribute derived from the form/field max_length (matching behavior prior to the regression). Example: <input type="text" name="username" maxlength="150" ...> (value depends on configured max_length).

5. Actual Behavior
The rendered username <input> does not include any maxlength attribute.

6. Severity/Priority
Severity: Medium
Priority: High for a regression fix (affects HTML rendering and backwards compatibility for many authentication forms).

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Projects using Django's AuthenticationForm (default auth views/forms).
- Applications that rely on client-side maxlength for validation or HTML validators.
- Likely affects Django versions including the regression commit (reported around Django 2.1).

8. Environment
- Regression introduced in commit 5ceaf14686ce626404afb6a5fbd3d8286410bf13 and pull request #27515.
- Reported against Django 2.1 (and any subsequent versions that include the commit).
- Relevant environments: any project rendering AuthenticationForm in templates; Python version not specifically implicated.

9. Additional Information
- Related discussion threads:
  - https://groups.google.com/forum/?utm_source=digest&utm_medium=email#!topic/django-developers/qnfSqro0DlA
  - https://forum.djangoproject.com/t/possible-authenticationform-max-length-regression-in-django-2-1/241
- Regression commit: 5ceaf14686ce626404afb6a5fbd3d8286410bf13
- Pull request/issue reference: #27515
- Potential area to inspect: how widget attributes (attrs) are populated for AuthenticationForm/username field rendering following the change in the referenced commit.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Migrations serialize Enum default using Enum value (translated string) instead of Enum name, causing ValueError after translation

2. Description
When an Enum member instance (from enum.Enum) is used as the default value for a CharField and the Enum member values are translation-wrapped (e.g., gettext_lazy), the generated migration file serializes the default by the Enum value (the translated string) rather than by the Enum name. After translations are applied, the serialized value no longer matches any Enum member value and old migrations fail with ValueError when applied or inspected.

3. Steps to Reproduce
1. Define an Enum with translation-wrapped values and override __str__ to return the name:
   from enum import Enum
   from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _
   class Status(Enum):
       GOOD = _('Good')
       BAD = _('Bad')
       def __str__(self):
           return self.name
2. Use an Enum member as a default for a CharField in a model:
   class Item(models.Model):
       status = models.CharField(default=Status.GOOD, max_length=128)
3. Run makemigrations to generate a migration.
4. Observe generated migration contains code like:
   ('status', models.CharField(default=Status('Good'), max_length=128))
5. Enable or change translations so _('Good') is translated to another language (so the value becomes e.g. 'Bueno').
6. Run or inspect migrations; Django raises:
   ValueError: 'Good' is not a valid Status
   (or after translation, 'Bueno' is not a valid Status)

4. Expected Behavior
Migrations should serialize the Enum default by a stable identifier that does not change with translation, e.g. by the Enum member name:
('status', models.CharField(default=Status['GOOD'], max_length=128))
This representation remains valid regardless of translations of the Enum value.

5. Actual Behavior
Migrations serialize the Enum default by calling the Enum with its value:
('status', models.CharField(default=Status('Good'), max_length=128))
Because the Enum value is translation-wrapped and can change per-language, previously generated migration files can become invalid when translations change or are applied.

6. Severity/Priority
High — This breaks existing migrations for projects that use translated Enum values as defaults, causing migration files to become non-replayable and raising runtime errors.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Django projects that:
  - Use Python enum.Enum members as default values for model fields (e.g., CharField),
  - Have Enum values wrapped in gettext_lazy or other translation facilities,
  - Rely on generated migration files to be stable across locales/time.
- Any system that runs makemigrations in an environment with translatable Enum values.

8. Environment
- Python: enum.Enum (Python 3.x)
- Django: migration system (makemigrations) — specific Django version not provided in report; issue affects migration serialization behavior.
- i18n: gettext_lazy (django.utils.translation.gettext_lazy) or other lazy translation wrappers.
- Models: CharField default set to an Enum member instance.

9. Additional Information
- Example error: ValueError: 'Good' is not a valid Status (or, after translation, ValueError: 'TranslatedWord' is not a valid Status).
- Suggested behavior/fix: When serializing Enum members in migrations, use a representation based on the Enum member name (e.g., Status['GOOD']) or otherwise serialize a stable identifier (name) rather than the potentially-translated value. This ensures migration files remain valid regardless of translations.
- Workarounds: Avoid using translated Enum values as direct defaults in model fields; use the Enum name or a non-translated value as the default, or supply a callable default that resolves to the correct Enum at runtime.

problem_statement:
1. Title
models.E015 raised when Meta.ordering contains "__pk" of a related field (e.g. "option__pk")

2. Description
When a model's Meta.ordering includes a lookup that ends with "__pk" for a related field (for example "option__pk"), Django raises models.E015, claiming the ordering refers to a nonexistent field, related field, or lookup. This is a regression introduced in commit 440505cb2cadbe1a5b9fba246bcde6c04f51d07e. The ordering should accept related primary-key lookups (related__pk) and not produce this validation error.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Define two models where one has a ForeignKey to the other, e.g.:
  - class Option(models.Model): ...
  - class SomeModel(models.Model):
      option = models.ForeignKey(Option, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
      class Meta:
          ordering = ['option__pk']
- Run model validation (for example: python manage.py check or any code path that validates model options).
- Observe the error.

Example error message observed:
test_app.SomeModel: (models.E015) 'ordering' refers to the nonexistent field, related field, or lookup 'option__pk'.

4. Expected Behavior
Meta.ordering that contains related primary-key lookups such as "related_field__pk" should be accepted as valid and not trigger models.E015. The system should treat "__pk" on related fields as a valid lookup for ordering.

5. Actual Behavior
models.E015 is raised indicating the ordering entry refers to a nonexistent field, related field, or lookup (e.g. 'option__pk'), preventing intended use of related pk lookups in Meta.ordering.

6. Severity/Priority
Severity: Medium — breaks valid model configurations and causes errors during model validation/checks.
Priority: High for users relying on related__pk in ordering; Medium overall because it is a regression.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Projects that use Meta.ordering containing related primary-key lookups (e.g. 'related__pk').
- Any code paths that run Django's model validation/checks (manage.py check, app loading, migrations that validate models).

8. Environment
- Regression introduced in commit: 440505cb2cadbe1a5b9fba246bcde6c04f51d07e
- Affects the Django codebase at or after the above commit. (No specific Django release number provided in the report.)

9. Additional Information
- The issue is specific to lookups ending in "__pk" on related fields inside Meta.ordering; other valid ordering entries should continue to work.
- A minimal reproduction is provided in Steps to Reproduce. Fix should restore previous behavior where related__pk is recognized as a valid lookup for ordering.

problem_statement:
1. Title
django.utils.http.parse_http_date incorrectly interprets two-digit RFC850 years using a hard-coded pivot

2. Description
The current implementation of django.utils.http.parse_http_date maps two-digit RFC850 years using a hard-coded rule (00–69 → 2000–2069, 70–99 → 1970–1999). RFC 7231 requires that recipients interpret a two-digit year by comparing against the current date: if the interpreted year appears to be more than 50 years in the future, it must be treated as the most recent past year with the same last two digits. The hard-coded mapping will become incorrect as time advances and should instead compute the century relative to the current year (the 50-year rule).

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Construct an RFC850-style date string with a two-digit year, for example: "Sunday, 06-Nov-70 08:49:37 GMT".
- Ensure the system/current-year context is a year where the hard-coded mapping differs from the 50-year rule decision (e.g., simulate current year 2071).
- Call django.utils.http.parse_http_date("Sunday, 06-Nov-70 08:49:37 GMT").
- Observe the returned epoch/year.

4. Expected Behavior
The function should apply RFC 7231’s rule: choose the century so that the resulting year is not more than 50 years in the future relative to the current date. In the example with current year 2071, the two-digit year "70" should be interpreted as 2070 (not 1970), because 2070 is recent and 1970 is >50 years in the past.

5. Actual Behavior
The function uses the static rule 00–69 → 2000–2069 and 70–99 → 1970–1999, so it would interpret "70" as 1970 regardless of the current year. As time passes, this hard-coded pivot causes incorrect century selection and wrong timestamps.

6. Severity/Priority
Medium-High. Misinterpreting dates can cause incorrect caching behavior, wrong conditional request handling, and other errors in components that rely on accurate parsing of HTTP date headers.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Django applications that parse HTTP date headers via django.utils.http.parse_http_date.
- Caching, conditional GET/If-Modified-Since logic, Expires/Last-Modified handling, middleware and any third-party packages that rely on this function.

8. Environment
- Function: django.utils.http.parse_http_date
- Affects Django versions where parse_http_date implements the hard-coded 00–69/70–99 logic (exact versions to be confirmed).
- Behavior independent of Python interpreter version; depends on how current year is obtained at runtime.

9. Additional Information
- RFC 7231 excerpt: "Recipients of a timestamp value in rfc850-date format, which uses a two-digit year, MUST interpret a timestamp that appears to be more than 50 years in the future as representing the most recent year in the past that had the same last two digits."
- Recommended fix: compute the full year relative to the current year using a +/-50 year pivot (or equivalent algorithm) rather than a fixed 1970/2000 break point.
- Example failing scenario: with current year 2071, parse_http_date currently returns 1970 for two-digit "70" but RFC 7231 requires interpreting it as 2070.

problem_statement:
1. Title
FormField.__deepcopy__ performs a shallow copy and causes error_messages dict to be shared between field copies

2. Description
The __deepcopy__ implementation for form fields performs only a shallow copy of self and does not deep-copy the error_messages dictionary. As a result, multiple copies of the same Field instance share the same error_messages mapping. If a Form or ModelForm modifies a field's error_messages dynamically (e.g., in __init__), that change is reflected across all copies and instances that share the field, producing incorrect or leaked validation messages across form instances. This behavior has been observed at least as far back as Django 1.11.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Define a Form subclass with a field that has an error_messages dictionary.
- In the Form (or a subclass) modify that field's error_messages in runtime (for example, in __init__ set self.fields['name'].error_messages['required'] = 'Custom required message').
- Instantiate two separate form instances of the same Form class.
- Observe that modifying error_messages on the field in one instance also changes it in the other instance (the second instance unexpectedly sees the modified message).

Minimal reproduction sketch:
- class ProfileForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField(error_messages={'required': 'Name required'})
- f1 = ProfileForm()
  f2 = ProfileForm()
- f1.fields['name'].error_messages['required'] = 'Custom message'
- Now f2.fields['name'].error_messages['required'] == 'Custom message' (unexpected)

4. Expected Behavior
Each form instance should have its own independent copy of fields (including their error_messages) such that modifying error_messages on a field within one form instance does not affect other form instances or other copies of the same field. __deepcopy__ on Field should produce an independent error_messages dict (deep copy) so per-instance modifications are isolated.

5. Actual Behavior
Field.__deepcopy__ performs a shallow copy and does not create a separate copy of the error_messages dictionary. Consequently, the error_messages dict is shared between copies and changes made to one copy's error_messages appear in all copies and instances that share the original field.

6. Severity/Priority
High / Major — causes state leakage between form instances, leading to incorrect validation messages and potential confusion in applications that dynamically modify field error messages.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Developers who modify form field error_messages dynamically (common in Forms and ModelForms).
- Any Django application using per-instance customization of field error messages.
- Confirmed for Django versions back to 1.11; likely affects other versions with the same implementation.

8. Environment
- Django repository reference: fields.py __deepcopy__ implementation (example link: https://github.com/django/django/blob/146086f219d01dbb1cd8c089b5a5667e396e1cc4/django/forms/fields.py#L200)
- Observed in Django 1.11 and in later commits that retain the same deepcopy behavior (commit id referenced above).
- Python versions not specifically required; problem is in Django form code.

9. Additional Information
- Root cause: __deepcopy__ does a shallow clone of self and does not explicitly deepcopy mutable attributes like error_messages.
- Suggested fix: update Field.__deepcopy__ to deepcopy the error_messages dict (and any other mutable attributes that should be per-copy) when creating the copy.
- Backward compatibility: changing to deep copy error_messages should align with expected per-instance isolation of Form fields, but review for any code that relies on sharing error_messages across copies (unlikely).
- Relevant code locations: django/forms/fields.py __deepcopy__ and django/forms/forms.py where fields are copied for form instances.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Combine fast delete queries by table when emulating ON DELETE CASCADE

2. Description
When emulating ON DELETE CASCADE via on_delete=models.CASCADE, deletion.Collector uses a "fast" path that issues DELETE FROM table WHERE pk IN (...) or DELETE FROM table WHERE fk = :id. When multiple fast-path deletes target the same table (for example different foreign-key columns or both sides of a many-to-many join table), the collector currently emits separate DELETE statements per relation/column. These should be combined into a single DELETE per table (using OR between column predicates or IN for pks) to reduce database roundtrips and improve delete performance.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Define the following models:
  - Person with friends = ManyToManyField('self')
  - User
  - Entry with created_by = ForeignKey(User) and updated_by = ForeignKey(User)
- Create a User and related Entry rows and Person rows with M2M links.
- Call person.delete() or user.delete() or delete a User instance via the ORM.
- Observe SQL emitted by the deletion. Example observed statements:
  - DELETE FROM person_friends WHERE from_id = :id
  - DELETE FROM person_friends WHERE to_id = :id
  - DELETE FROM person WHERE id = :id
  - DELETE FROM entry WHERE created_by_id = :id
  - DELETE FROM entry WHERE updated_by_id = :id
  - DELETE FROM user WHERE id = :id

4. Expected Behavior
When multiple fast-path delete queries target the same table during cascade emulation, the collector should combine them into a single DELETE per table. Example combined statements:
  - DELETE FROM person_friends WHERE from_id = :id OR to_id = :id
  - DELETE FROM entry WHERE created_by_id = :id OR updated_by_id = :id
Other DELETEs (e.g., DELETE FROM person WHERE id = :id and DELETE FROM user WHERE id = :id) remain unchanged.

5. Actual Behavior
The collector emits separate DELETE statements for each relation/column that qualifies for the fast path, resulting in multiple roundtrips for the same table (one per relation/column).

6. Severity/Priority

problem_statement:
1. Title
bulk_create batch_size param overrides the compatible batch size calculation

2. Description
In Django stable/2.2.x, the bulk_create implementation uses the supplied batch_size parameter directly, overriding the internally calculated compatible max_batch_size. This appears to be a bug because bulk_update already enforces the smaller of the two values. The behavior can cause oversized batches to be sent to the database (potentially exceeding DB parameter limits). Suggested fix: apply the same min(batch_size, max_batch_size) if batch_size else max_batch_size logic used in bulk_update.

3. Steps to Reproduce
1. Define a model with multiple fields such that INSERT statements use many SQL parameters.
2. Create a large list of model instances to insert.
3. Call Model.objects.bulk_create(objs, batch_size=some_large_value) where some_large_value is greater than the internally computed max_batch_size.
4. Observe that bulk_create uses the provided batch_size directly, which may produce an INSERT that exceeds the database parameter/placeholder limits or otherwise results in oversized batches or errors.

4. Expected Behavior
When a caller supplies a batch_size to bulk_create, Django should respect the database-compatible maximum batch size and use the minimum of the provided batch_size and the computed max_batch_size. In other words:
batch_size = min(batch_size, max_batch_size) if batch_size else max_batch_size

5. Actual Behavior
bulk_create uses the supplied batch_size value without taking the computed max_batch_size into account, allowing batch sizes that may be incompatible with the database's parameter/placeholder limits.

6. Severity/Priority
High — this can lead to runtime errors (e.g., "too many SQL variables" or similar DB errors) or failed bulk inserts for users relying on batch_size with models that generate many SQL parameters.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Applications using Django stable/2.2.x.
- Users calling QuerySet.bulk_create with a batch_size argument.
- Environments with databases that have limits on the number of SQL parameters/placeholders (e.g., SQLite, some configurations of other DB backends).

8. Environment
- Django: stable/2.2.x
- File references:
  - bulk_create location: django/db/models/query.py (approx. line referenced in report)
  - bulk_update comparator logic: django/db/models/query.py (bulk_update implementation reference)
- Database backend: any backend with parameter/placeholder limits (behavior observed when batch_size > computed max_batch_size).

9. Additional Information
- Original reporter: (last modified by Ahmet Kucuk)
- Relevant lines in repository:
  - bulk_create reference: https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/2.2.x/django/db/models/query.py#L1197
  - bulk_update reference: https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/2.2.x/django/db/models/query.py#L504
- Proposed fix (same approach as bulk_update):
  batch_size = min(batch_size, max_batch_size) if batch_size else max_batch_size
- I am happy to open a pull request implementing this change.

problem_statement:
1. Title
Inconsistent type for TextChoices/IntegerChoices field value between newly created and retrieved model instances

2. Description
When a model CharField/IntegerField uses Django's TextChoices/IntegerChoices for choices, assigning an Enum member to the field on object creation yields an enum.Enum value on the in-memory instance, but retrieving the same object from the database returns the underlying raw value (str/int). This leads to inconsistent types and differing results from str(...) between freshly created instances and retrieved instances (e.g. "MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE" vs "first"), which can break downstream code or external API communication.

3. Steps to Reproduce
1. Define a TextChoices subclass and a model that uses it for a CharField:
   from django.db import models
   from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _
   class MyChoice(models.TextChoices):
       FIRST_CHOICE = "first", _("The first choice, it is")
       SECOND_CHOICE = "second", _("The second choice, it is")
   class MyObject(models.Model):
       my_str_value = models.CharField(max_length=10, choices=MyChoice.choices)
2. Create an instance using an enum member:
   self.my_object = MyObject.objects.create(my_str_value=MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE)
3. Inspect the in-memory instance:
   isinstance(self.my_object.my_str_value, str) -> False
   str(self.my_object.my_str_value) -> "MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE"
4. Retrieve the instance from the DB:
   my_object = MyObject.objects.last()
   isinstance(my_object.my_str_value, str) -> True
   str(my_object.my_str_value) -> "first"
5. Run the provided tests to observe a failing assertion:
   ./manage.py test

4. Expected Behavior
The field value should have a consistent type whether it is on a freshly created in-memory model instance or on an instance retrieved from the database. Ideally:
- Assigning MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE should result in the stored and exposed value being the underlying raw value ("first"), and str(...) should produce "first" in both cases.
- Alternatively, if the field exposes enum members, both created and retrieved instances should expose enum members consistently.

5. Actual Behavior
- Newly created in-memory instance: the field getter returns an enum.Enum member; str(...) yields "MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE".
- Retrieved instance from the database: the field getter returns the raw underlying value (a str "first").
This mismatch causes tests and code relying on the field string value to fail (see assertion error: 'MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE' != 'first').

6. Severity/Priority
High — causes data-type mismatches and unexpected serialization differences that can break integrations (APIs) and tests.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Django applications using TextChoices or IntegerChoices with CharField/IntegerField and assigning Enum members directly when creating model instances.
- Any code that serializes model instances (especially freshly created ones) to external systems expecting the raw choice value.

8. Environment
- Observed in a Django 3.0 environment (reference: django30-venv, manage.py test).
- Example run output shows the failing test on a developer macOS path: /Users/mikailkocak/Development/django30/.
- Python version not specified in the report; reproduce with the Django 3.0 test setup.

9. Additional Information
- The differing behavior is visible in the provided test case (EnumTest) where test_created_object_is_str fails while test_retrieved_object_is_str passes.
- The root symptom: enum.Enum.__str__ returns a "Class.member" representation, while the database stores and returns the raw value (value attribute of the enum). The in-memory assignment appears not to be normalized to the raw value before exposure.
- Potential immediate workarounds: assign the raw value directly (MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE.value or "first") when creating instances, or normalize the field value after creation.
- Full failing assertion excerpt:
  AssertionError: 'MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE' != 'first'

1. Title
Cannot override get_FOO_display() on model fields in Django 2.2 and later

2. Description
In Django 2.2+ I am unable to override the automatically provided get_<fieldname>_display() method on model instances. The same override works in Django 2.1. When I define a custom get_foo_bar_display() on the model, Django 2.2+ still returns the choices label produced by Django's built-in implementation instead of calling my override.

3. Steps to Reproduce
- Create a Django app and a model like:
  class FooBar(models.Model):
      foo_bar = models.CharField(_("foo"), choices=[(1, 'foo'), (2, 'bar')])
      def __str__(self):
          return self.get_foo_bar_display()
      def get_foo_bar_display(self):
          return "something"
- Migrate and create an instance in the database (e.g., FooBar.objects.create(foo_bar=1)).
- From Django shell or template, call str(instance) or instance.get_foo_bar_display().

4. Expected Behavior
The model's custom get_foo_bar_display() method should be called. str(instance) and instance.get_foo_bar_display() should return "something" (the overridden value).

5. Actual Behavior
On Django 2.2 and later, str(instance) and instance.get_foo_bar_display() return the choices label ("foo" or "bar") produced by Django's built-in implementation, not the custom "something" value. In Django 2.1 the same code correctly returned "something".

6. Severity/Priority
Medium to High - This is a regression from Django 2.1 that breaks codebases that rely on overriding get_<field>_display() on models. It can affect display logic and may require workarounds in multiple places.

7. Affected Users/Systems
- Developers who override get_<fieldname>_display() on Django model classes.
- Django applications upgraded from 2.1 to 2.2+ that rely on such overrides for display or stringification logic.

8. Environment
- Django 2.2 and later: issue observed (regression).
- Django 2.1: expected behavior (override works).
- Python and OS not specified in original report; issue appears framework-version dependent and not environment-specific.

9. Additional Information
- Minimal reproducible example supplied above.
- The expected behavior is that model-defined methods should take precedence over auto-generated methods for field display. A fix or guidance on the intended behavior and recommended workaround (if any) would be helpful.

OK, so there is a behaviour change here, but Sergey is correct that it does depend on attr order, so it's hard to say that this can be said to ever have been thought of as supported, with the exact example provided. This example produces the opposite result on 2.1 (even on >=PY36): def test_overriding_display_backwards(self): class FooBar2(models.Model): def get_foo_bar_display(self): return "something" foo_bar = models.CharField("foo", choices=[(1, 'foo'), (2, 'bar')]) f = FooBar2(foo_bar=1) # This returns 'foo' or 'bar' in both 2.2 and 2.1 self.assertEqual(f.get_foo_bar_display(), "foo") Because get_foo_bar_display() is defined before foo_bar is gets replaced in the the add_to_class() step. Semantically order shouldn't make a difference. Given that it does, I can't see that we're bound to maintain that behaviour. (There's a possible fix in Field.contribute_to_class() but implementing that just reverses the pass/fail behaviour depending on order...) Rather, the correct way to implement this on 2.2+ is: def test_overriding_display(self): class FooBar(models.Model): foo_bar = models.CharField("foo", choices=[(1, 'foo'), (2, 'bar')]) def _get_FIELD_display(self, field): if field.attname == 'foo_bar': return "something" return super()._get_FIELD_display(field) f = FooBar(foo_bar=1) self.assertEqual(f.get_foo_bar_display(), "something") This is stable for declaration order on version 2.2+. This approach requires overriding _get_FIELD_display() before declaring fields on 2.1, because otherwise Model._get_FIELD_display() is picked up during Field.contribute_to_class(). This ordering dependency is, ultimately, the same issue that was addressed in a68ea231012434b522ce45c513d84add516afa60, and the follow-up in #30254. The behaviour in 2.1 (and before) was incorrect. Yes, there's a behaviour change here but it's a bugfix, and all bugfixes are breaking changes if you're depending on the broken behaviour. I'm going to downgrade this from Release Blocker accordingly. I'll reclassify this as a Documentation issue and provide the working example, as overriding _get_FIELD_display() is a legitimate use-case I'd guess.
